description: Imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention and positive thinking applied to sporting performance.
content_html:
The Mental Side of Sport

Physical fitness and technical skill are not enough to guarantee peak performance. Elite athletes consistently report that the mental dimension of their preparation is as important as their physical training. Missing a penalty, misjudging a serve at a crucial moment, or freezing under pressure before a major competition — these experiences are not failures of technique alone. They reflect psychological factors that can be trained and managed. OCR identifies four mental preparation techniques that performers use to optimise their psychological readiness: imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention and positive thinking. Each technique addresses a different aspect of the performer’s mental state, and together they form a practical toolkit for performance preparation.

Imagery

Imagery is the deliberate creation of vivid mental pictures associated with sport. Unlike simply “thinking about” a sport, effective imagery engages multiple senses — the sound of the crowd, the texture of the ball, the sensation of the playing surface underfoot, the feeling of muscles working at full effort. A long-jumper preparing to compete might use imagery to experience, in vivid detail, the feeling of the approach run, the plant foot striking the board, the explosive drive of the hips and the moment of landing. A basketball player might image the sound of the ball swishing through the net.

Imagery works because the brain’s response to a vividly imagined experience shares many of the same neural pathways as the actual experience. Detailed, multi-sensory imaging creates a mental state of readiness that bridges the gap between preparation and competition. Imagery can also be used to manage nerves — a performer who has repeatedly imaged calm, controlled execution in a high-pressure moment is less likely to feel the situation as novel or overwhelming when it arrives. Adam Peaty has described using detailed imagery before major championship heats, imprinting a sense of familiarity onto what would otherwise feel like unique, high-stakes moments.

Mental Rehearsal

Mental rehearsal is the internal simulation of a complete performance or skill sequence, carried out in the mind before physical execution. Where imagery is primarily about creating a sensory experience, mental rehearsal has a more structured, procedural focus: the performer runs through the exact sequence of movements they intend to execute, in correct order, as if previewing the performance from inside their own body.

A diver performing a new list of dives at a national competition would use mental rehearsal to run through each dive in the correct sequence — approach, hurdle step, take-off, tuck position, entry — several times before mounting the board. Research shows that mentally rehearsed movements activate many of the same motor pathways as physically performed movements, effectively providing “practice” that reinforces the movement programme without physical effort or risk. Mental rehearsal is most effective when performed in real time (not rushed), in the first person (from the performer’s own perspective), and always picturing successful execution rather than errors.

Key Fact

Imagery creates a vivid multi-sensory experience of sport, engaging feelings, sounds and visual detail — it prepares the mind for the competitive environment. Mental rehearsal is a structured run-through of the skill sequence itself, rehearsing the exact movement programme before physical execution. Both techniques are used in the period before competition. Both picture success, never failure.

Selective Attention

Selective attention is the skill of directing focus towards the information that matters and filtering out everything else. Competition environments are full of potential distractions: crowd noise, opponents’ behaviour, negative internal thoughts, environmental conditions. A performer who has not trained their attention will find that these distractions invade their focus at precisely the moments when concentration is most critical.

Training selective attention means deliberately practising the ability to lock onto task-relevant cues — the flight of the ball, the position of a defender, the feel of the racket at contact — while choosing to ignore everything else. A tennis player preparing to receive a serve must direct all attention to the server’s ball toss and racket path, blocking out crowd noise, score awareness and anxiety about the point. A sprinter in the blocks must focus on the starting gun and their own movement activation, filtering out lane-side distractions and the presence of rivals. Dina Asher-Smith has spoken about developing a “tunnel vision” process in the call room before major finals, systematically narrowing attention to her own race plan.

Selective attention is developed through repeated practice, cueing routines (where the performer identifies specific cues to focus on) and mental preparation before competition. It is closely linked to both imagery and positive thinking — a performer who has imaged the task clearly and has a positive mental script is better able to focus on task-relevant cues because there is less cognitive space for distractions to fill.

Positive Thinking

Positive thinking involves consciously replacing negative internal dialogue with prepared, constructive thoughts. In sport, negative thinking is extremely common: “I always miss these”, “I’ve never done well in this arena”, “everyone is watching me”. Left unchallenged, negative thoughts reduce confidence, tighten muscles, narrow attention in unhelpful ways and can trigger the self-fulfilling prophecy of poor performance. Positive thinking is the deliberate psychological counterattack.

The technique works by having the performer prepare a set of positive, task-focused mental statements in advance of competition. These statements are not empty slogans but specific, believable reminders that redirect attention towards what the performer can do: “I have trained this kick hundreds of times”, “I trust my technique”, “smooth contact, follow through”. When negative thoughts arise — and in high-pressure moments they will — the performer activates their prepared positive script, interrupting the negative loop and redirecting focus to the execution cues.

Positive thinking does not require ignoring difficulty or pretending a situation is not pressured. It is realistic self-support: acknowledging the importance of the moment while maintaining belief in preparation. A rugby goal kicker who thinks “this kick matters AND I have the skill to execute it” is using positive thinking effectively. A kicker who tells themselves “this is fine, I never miss” when their recent form has been poor is not — that is denial, which collapses under real pressure.

Elite athletes rarely use just one mental preparation technique in isolation. Before a major competition, a gymnast might use mental rehearsal (running through the floor routine in sequence), imagery (experiencing the feel and sound of the hall and the sensation of the tumble run), selective attention (narrowing focus to the floor and the music, filtering out the score and the audience), and positive thinking (“I have trained this routine for six months — my body knows what to do”). Together, the four techniques create a psychological state of readiness in which the performer is fully focused on successful execution. In an exam, you may be asked to explain how one specific technique works or to evaluate the relative usefulness of the four techniques — make sure you can describe the mechanism of each separately before discussing how they combine.

Key Fact

Four OCR mental preparation techniques: (1) Imagery — vivid multi-sensory mental pictures that prepare the mind for competition. (2) Mental rehearsal — a structured run-through of the skill sequence in the mind before physical execution. (3) Selective attention — focusing on task-relevant cues while filtering out distractions. (4) Positive thinking — replacing negative internal dialogue with prepared positive scripts to maintain confidence.

OCR’s sports psychology unit covers the four techniques above and no more in this section. The following topics appear on other examination boards but are NOT assessed by OCR and should not appear in your answers: arousal and the inverted-U theory; information processing models; personality types; aggression types; motivation types; contract to compete. If a question asks you about mental preparation in sport, restrict your answer to imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention and positive thinking. Adding content from outside the OCR specification will not gain marks and may suggest to the examiner that you are confused about the scope of the course.
exam_tip_html: On 4-mark explain questions about mental preparation, the most common error is describing a technique without explaining why it works. Writing “the athlete uses imagery to picture themselves succeeding” earns only 1 mark. To earn the full 4, you must also explain the mechanism — “imagery activates similar neural pathways to physical performance, creating a sense of familiarity with the competitive situation and building confidence before the event” — and apply it to the specific scenario in the question. On the 8-mark evaluate question, always ensure you cover all four techniques (or at least three) and that you consider both the benefits and any limitations. OCR’s levels-based mark scheme rewards range, balance and sporting application. A common pitfall is writing only about one technique in depth — that approach will cap your mark in the lower bands. Use a ‘For X... However Y...’ structure for each technique, anchored to a named sporting example.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • OCR identifies four mental preparation techniques: imagery (vivid multi-sensory mental pictures), mental rehearsal (structured internal run-through of the skill sequence), selective attention (filtering out distractions to focus on task cues), and positive thinking (replacing negative thoughts with prepared positive scripts).
  • Mental rehearsal is most effective when performed in real time, first-person and always picturing successful execution — not errors.
  • The four techniques are often used together and reinforce each other; athletes develop them through deliberate practice as a core part of their preparation routine.

practice_questions.text: Identify one mental preparation technique a penalty taker in football might use in the moments before striking the ball.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of the following: imagery (1); mental rehearsal (1); selective attention (1); positive thinking (1). Accept brief descriptions that clearly identify one of the four named techniques. Do not credit arousal management, deep breathing or other techniques not on the OCR specification.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'selective attention' in the context of sporting performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core idea: selective attention is the ability to focus on relevant information during performance. 1 mark for the second dimension: blocking out or filtering out irrelevant distractions (such as crowd noise, opponent behaviour or anxiety) that are not useful to the execution of the skill.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a county-level diver could use mental rehearsal to prepare for a new dive in competition.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that mental rehearsal involves running through the skill sequence internally before physical execution (1). 1 mark for describing the process: the diver runs through each phase of the dive in order (approach, hurdle step, take-off, tuck, entry) in real time, from a first-person perspective, picturing successful execution (1). 1 mark for the benefit: rehearsing the movement activates similar motor pathways to physical practice, reinforcing the movement programme and building familiarity without physical effort or injury risk (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how positive thinking could help a club-level rugby goal kicker maintain performance under pressure during a high-stakes conversion attempt.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that positive thinking involves replacing negative internal thoughts with prepared positive statements (1). 1 mark for the mechanism: negative thoughts (e.g. 'I always miss under pressure') are interrupted by a prepared positive script, redirecting attention from feared outcomes to execution cues (1). 1 mark for application: the kicker uses a statement such as 'I have practised this kick hundreds of times' or 'trust my technique' to maintain focus on the process (1). 1 mark for the outcome: confidence is maintained, muscles remain relaxed, and the execution cues rather than the outcome drive the performance (1).

practice_questions.text: A club-level gymnast is preparing for her first national competition. Her coach suggests she incorporates all four mental preparation techniques into her warm-up routine. Evaluate how effective each technique could be in helping her perform at her best.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation addressing all four techniques, considering both benefits and limitations for this gymnast scenario, with a justified conclusion. Arguments for imagery: creates multi-sensory familiarity with the competitive hall and the routine before physical execution, reducing the novelty of the competitive environment; limitation: requires skill to generate detailed imagery — a performer new to the technique may struggle to produce vivid, stable mental pictures. Arguments for mental rehearsal: activates motor pathways and reinforces the floor routine sequence without physical fatigue; first-competition nerves may cause rehearsal to be rushed or to drift to negative outcomes if not carefully managed. Arguments for selective attention: narrows focus to the floor and the music, filtering out judge presence and crowd noise — critical for a first national appearance; limitation: developing attention control takes time and practice; it cannot be fully acquired the week before competition. Arguments for positive thinking: interrupts performance anxiety and refocuses the gymnast on what she can do; limitation: statements must be believable — hollow reassurance collapses under real pressure. Conclusion: all four techniques contribute and they work best in combination; selective attention and positive thinking are most immediately deployable, while imagery and mental rehearsal require more practice to be fully effective. Consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure: Addresses at least three techniques with mostly developed points on both sides. Mostly applied to the gymnast scenario. Reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Addresses two or three techniques but one-sided (mostly benefits); thin application or limited development.

Emerging: Names one or two techniques; descriptive rather than evaluative; little sporting application.

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which imagery differs from mental rehearsal as mental preparation techniques.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct differences: imagery focuses on vivid multi-sensory experience (feelings, sounds, sights of the performance environment), while mental rehearsal is a structured run-through of the movement sequence (1); imagery creates mental familiarity with the competitive environment and emotional state, while mental rehearsal rehearses the exact procedural movement programme (1); imagery is broader and sensory, while mental rehearsal is procedural and movement-focused (1). Maximum 2 marks; do not credit the same distinction twice.

knowledge_checks.q: Which mental preparation technique involves running through the exact movement sequence in the mind before physical execution?
A tennis player blocking out crowd noise and focusing only on the server's ball toss is an example of which mental preparation technique?
Positive thinking involves replacing _____ internal dialogue with prepared, constructive statements.
Imagery works in part because vividly imagined movement activates similar _____ pathways to those used in physical performance.
Match each mental preparation technique to the correct description of how it helps performance:
right: Filters out distractions to focus on task-relevant cues
Replaces negative thoughts with affirming statements to maintain confidence
Creates vivid multi-sensory mental pictures to prepare the mind for competition

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four OCR mental preparation techniques?
flashcard_questions.a: Imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention, positive thinking.

flashcard_questions.q: What is imagery as a mental preparation technique?
flashcard_questions.a: Creating vivid multi-sensory mental pictures related to sport to prepare the mind for competition.

flashcard_questions.q: What is mental rehearsal in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: An internal run-through of the skill sequence in the mind before physical execution.

flashcard_questions.q: For mental rehearsal to be most effective, it should be performed how?
flashcard_questions.a: In real time, first-person perspective, always picturing successful execution.

flashcard_questions.q: What is selective attention in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: The ability to focus on relevant information and block out distractions during performance.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one sporting example of selective attention in action.
flashcard_questions.a: A sprinter in the blocks focusing only on the starter's gun, filtering out rivals and crowd noise.

flashcard_questions.q: What is positive thinking as a mental preparation technique?
flashcard_questions.a: Deliberately replacing negative thoughts with prepared positive, affirming statements.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is positive thinking more than just saying 'it will be fine'?
flashcard_questions.a: Statements must be specific and believable; hollow reassurance collapses under real pressure.

flashcard_questions.q: How does imagery help reduce pre-competition nerves?
flashcard_questions.a: It makes the competitive environment feel familiar, reducing novelty and the associated anxiety.

flashcard_questions.q: How does mental rehearsal reinforce movement patterns without physical effort?
flashcard_questions.a: It activates similar motor pathways to physical practice, reinforcing the programme mentally.

flashcard_questions.q: Is arousal theory (inverted-U) part of OCR's mental preparation topic?
flashcard_questions.a: No - OCR only assesses the four named techniques: imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention, positive thinking.

flashcard_questions.q: Which four senses might a long-jumper use during imagery before competition?
flashcard_questions.a: Sight (visual run-up), feel (foot striking board), sound (crowd), sensation (muscular drive).

glossary_terms.definition: A mental technique in which a performer deliberately creates vivid sensory images related to sport, including feelings, sounds and visual details of a performance, to prepare the mind for competition.

A mental technique in which a performer creates an internal simulation of successfully executing a skill or performance, rehearsing the complete movement sequence in the mind before performing it physically.
The ability to focus on relevant information and block out distractions that are not useful to the performance of a skill.
A mental technique in which a performer deliberately replaces negative thoughts with positive, affirming statements or mental scripts, maintaining confidence and focus under pressure.
Psychological techniques used by performers to optimise their mental state before and during competition.
The specific pieces of information in the performance environment that a performer should focus on to execute a skill correctly, such as the flight of the ball or the position of a defender.

hero_image_caption: Mental preparation techniques help athletes channel focus and maintain confidence under competition pressure.
